content: The 2007 treatment guidelines from the American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) for the management of Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection outline specific indications for diagnosis and treatment. These include: 1. Active Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD): This applies to both gastric and duodenal ulcers. 2. History of Peptic Ulcer Disease: Patients with a confirmed history of PUD who have not previously been treated for H. pylori. 3. Gastric MALT Lymphoma: Specifically, low-grade mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma. 4. Post-Endoscopic Resection of Early Gastric Cancer (EGC): Treatment is recommended following the removal of early-stage gastric cancer via endoscopy. First-Line Treatment for H. pylori Infection Several combinations of proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), clarithromycin, and amoxicillin have received FDA approval for first-line treatment of H. pylori infection. A regimen consisting of a PPI, clarithromycin, and metronidazole is not FDA-approved. A combination of PPI, bismuth, tetracycline, and metronidazole prescribed separately is also not FDA-approved. However, a combination product called Pylera, which includes bismuth subcitrate, tetracycline, and metronidazole, used alongside a PPI for 10 days, is an FDA-approved regimen. Adjuvant Therapy Emerging evidence suggests that certain probiotic strains, such as Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium species, may have an inhibitory effect on H. pylori. These probiotics may also help reduce the side effects of eradication therapies and improve patient compliance with treatment. Diagnostic Testing Recommendations The American Journal of Gastroenterology guidelines recommend performing endoscopy in the following scenarios to rule out peptic ulcer disease, esophagogastric malignancy, or other rare upper gastrointestinal conditions: 1. Dyspeptic patients over 55 years of age. 2. Dyspeptic patients with alarm features, which include: Gastrointestinal bleeding. Anemia. Early satiety. Unexplained weight loss exceeding 10% of body weight. Progressive difficulty swallowing (dysphagia). Painful swallowing (odynophagia). Persistent vomiting. A family history of gastrointestinal cancer. A history of esophagogastric malignancy. Previously documented peptic ulcer, lymphadenopathy, or an abdominal mass. For patients aged 55 years or younger without alarm features, two management strategies are recommended: 1. Test-and-Treat Strategy: This involves using a validated noninvasive test, such as the urea breath test or stool antigen test, to detect H. pylori. If eradication is successful but symptoms persist, a trial of acid suppression therapy may be considered. This approach is preferable in populations with a moderate to high prevalence of H. pylori infection (≥10%). 2. Empiric Acid Suppression Therapy: A trial of proton pump inhibitor (PPI) therapy for 4–8 weeks is recommended in areas with a low prevalence of H. pylori infection. Follow-Up and Eradication Testing Repeat endoscopy is not recommended once a diagnosis of functional dyspepsia has been firmly established, unless new symptoms or alarm features develop. Testing to confirm H. pylori eradication is most accurate when performed four weeks after the completion of therapy.
